newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE - Sahara desert's hidden wealth streams toward Europe.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sahara desert's hidden wealth streams toward Europe.

text.p: Deep in Algeria's Sahara Desert the army of men cursed the heat. At 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) machinery and massive pipes turned blistering hot.

Across the border, in Morocco's central Taza region, heavy rains turned earth to bog, sucking at boots, making every step an effort. Floods blocked roads and destroyed more equipment being used on the same project.

But slowly the project -- the Maghreb-Europe gas pipeline -- has advanced from Algeria's Hassi R'mel gas field, through neighbouring Morocco to near Tangiers, to disappear under the Strait of Gibraltar, and run 270 km (170 miles) inland from Tarifa to the ancient Spanish city of Cordoba.

"While we have been building it, we have had everything -- heat, rain, floods, strong winds, freezing weather and even snow," Morocco's sector construction boss Miguel Angel Pellon told Reuters."But at least there's a feeling of satisfaction."

He was speaking just days before the scheduled opening on November 1 of the $1.88 billion pipeline, a 48-inch buried tunnel through which natural gas will be pumped at nearly 20 km per hour (12 mph) across 1,385 km (865 miles).
Behind the opening ceremony of the pipeline with a yearly capacity of 9.5 billion cubic metres, and the possible later lifting to 18 billion cubic metres, was a battle against odds.
Algeria is debt-ridden and prey to violence. Only earlier this month two more workers with the state oil and gas company Sonatrach were slain, near Laghouat, not far from Hassi R'mel.
Foreign workers too have died, their murders equally blamed on Moslem fundamentalists. No-go zones had to be imposed around the sensitive gas and oil regions.

But despite everything, the Algerian section with what one Algerian official termed "American heavy gun technology" provided by building contractor Bechtel, was completed more than three months ahead of schedule.

Relations between Algeria and Morocco also are cool because of the disputed Western Sahara. Their land border is shut and a coordination team was set up to link the Algeria and Morocco pipes, buried to an average depth of 2.5 metres (eight ft).

Common economic interest and growing demand for gas from Spain and Portugal, whom the line will initially feed, and later perhaps more of Europe, saw initial agreement in 1991 between Algeria's state firm Sonatrach and Spain's Enagas.
Accords followed between the energy ministers of Algeria, Morocco and Spain.

An army of workers was assembled in 1994. In Algeria headed by Sonatrach, and in Morocco, where the work was under Metragaz, headed by Ignacio Martinez Diaz, some 5,000 workers were taken on. For the Strait of Gibraltar, 450 people started, with another 1,200 in Spain.
Martinez Diaz said 80 percent were locals, employed on two-year contracts.

An armada of ships, fleets of lorries and special trains were put on standby as steel company blasted out miles of pipe. It involved Europipe (Germany-France), Ilvain (Italy), Ensidesa (Spain), GTS (France), Hoesch and Mannesmann (Germany).
Competition for the contracts to provide the total 632,260 tonnes of main piping was intense in Europe's steel industry.

"We have been able to cut...costs of this project compared to base estimates (because of this)," Martinez Diaz said. "The total cost for the Algerian, Moroccan and Spanish parties is $1.88 billion, instead of $2.1 billion originally forecast."
The first trench was dug in Algeria in June 1994. Ships from Dunkirk, Bremen, Taranto and Santander headed for Nador in Morocco, Mostaganem in Algeria, and Cadiz in Spain, for the offshore section.
In six construction camps dotted across North Africa, the harshness of battling tough terrain could often be felt.

"Life was hard. Living together seven days in seven wasn't easy. If someone didn't like the fish or omelette served up... They were not four-star restaurants but they were acceptable," said Moroccan construction manager Angel Pellon.
"But the camps had a small bar, ping-pong, television, the occasional film, billiards. The bedrooms were air-conditioned and there were showers."
Algeria hopes to double its present annual gas exports to 60 billion cubic metres by the year 2000, when one Algerian official said its oil and gas exports should earn $16 billion.
Morocco later will use gas from Hassi R'mel, including for electricity generation, when it has set up the infrastructure. Until then it will take a share of the income generated.
To the south of Hassi R'mel, another project is already under way. Britain's BP has a $3 billion deal with Sonatrach for gas exploration and development in the inhospitable desert.
If successful, another pipeline -- of around 500 km (310 miles) -- may be needed to carry more gas to Hassi R'mel and then to the homes and plants of Europe.
